title: sshole (sshhole.com)
comments: OK, I think I see what’s going on with this, in this configuration.The goal from an attacker’s perspective is to get this to be true: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash); $ret == $hash` when called by OpenSSH’s sshd. This is how sshd validates that the user logging in knew the account password.The `$hash` is the “settings” to the crypt call and will normally look like “$6$--gibberish” for users with passwords set, but could look like “*” or “!” for users not intended to be able to login.The bug is from the intersection of all of these things:1. musl can return “*” for errors, rather than leave the return value NULL. Other libc have adopted something like this too, but seem to use a different result “*0”.2. musl can also return “+” for errors, but only does so if $hash starts with “*”. This is intended to eliminate the possibility of an error causing `$ret == $hash` to be true, however it assumes that applications calling `crypt()` will set $pw and $hash to values corresponding to the `$ret == $hash` comparison to be made immediately afterwards.3. OpenSSH can be convinced to pass the hash of a different user if the hash is “*” or “!” to avoid timing attacks that can enumerate the user list, so it will set $pw and $hash to correspond to different users. $hash will be a real “$6$--gibberish” style hash in this case, and OpenSSH expects `crypt()` to either return NULL or return a hash string. But now there’s two hashes OpenSSH uses. It does: `$ret = crypt($pw, $hash2); $ret == $hash1`;4. This should normally not be a problem because OpenSSH will pass in valid $pw and $hash2 that should not lead to errors in hashing, so the $ret that musl generates should be a real hash that cannot match the “*” or “!” $hash1 for the login-disabled user. However as a DDoS mitigation, musl will return error if the password is too long when using SHA-2-based hashes (the default, it seems).5. This error will result in a non-NULL result of “*” or “+”. Since OpenSSH passed in a real hash ($hash2), musl will return “*”, which compares equal to the actual user hash $hash1 for the disabled-login user.The OpenSSL adjustment ensures a minimum hash length for the user before logging them in, even if crypt() succeeds somehow.reply

I think the conclusion that can be drawn from this is that the behavior of crypt() is howling-at-the-moon insane, and it should no longer be considered for any system built in this century, at least not without extensive wrappers that correct and normalize all these edge cases.reply
Conclusion is type safety is importantreply

In this particular case, it is type safe. NULL, by the C standard does not refer to an object. It means that every pointer in C is effectively an option type, which mean that a function that returns a pointer can return NULL for "no result", which, in the case of crypt() is perfectly adequate.It is the opposite that is unsafe, that is, when the returned value can't be NULL, but it stills returns a pointer. C++ has references in an attempt to fix this problem.Because C tends to prioritize performance over safety, a NULL pointer dereference is considered undefined behavior and the compiler can invoke nasal demons if it makes the code go faster, but with the right options, you can have it checked and invoke what in other languages would call a panic handler, but on UNIX is the SIGSEGV signal. You can then attach a debugger or read the core file and see what went wrong.Note: I am not talking about "char *" for strings, that one is unsafe, but NULL is not. It is just a special case of an option type, or a result type, or an error union. Modern languages just extended this idea to objects other than pointers, and with more than one type of error.reply

> It is just a special case of an option type, or a result type, or an error union.These are not the same, and your next sentence suggests why. Option has but a single error type, but result types and error unions allow arbitrary types of error.reply

> the compiler can invoke nasal demons if it makes the code go fasterI had never heard that phrase, and was delighted at the answer when I googled it its origin, thank you:http://www.catb.org/jargon/html/N/nasal-demons.html> “When the compiler encounters [a given undefined construct] it is legal for it to make demons fly out of your nose” (the implication is that the compiler may choose any arbitrarily bizarre way to interpret the code without violating the ANSI C standard)reply

However this is limited by the compiler's actual abilities and code. The C standard doesn't forbid nasal demons, but the compiler isn't programmed to invoke nasal demons and isn't running on hardware with that capability, so it won't happen.I've heard nasal demons invoked as a literal possibility. No they are not a literal possibility.reply
You might consider it type safe according to C's rules, but it is not type safe according to contemporary opinion because the success type and error type are the same.reply

> [...] because the success type and error type are the same.That's a bit weird?  In Rust, if you have an thing that returns Result<String, String> that's still type safe, even though success and error types are the same.I think I understand what you want to express, maybe.  You might say it's in-band vs out-of-band error signalling?reply

> In Rust, if you have an thing that returns Result<String, String> that's still type safe, even though success and error types are the same.These types are not the same:    Ok<String>
    Err<String>reply

first_paragraph:
Drop-in MacTCP replacement for System 6 / 68000 MacsA modern, memory-lean replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs running System 6.

MoofTCP is a drop-in replacement for Apple's MacTCP. Programs written for MacTCP run on it unchanged, but
underneath it is a fresh TCP/IP stack written from scratch in portable C, with its own control panel, installer
and DHCP client. It was built for a Mac Classic with 4 MB of RAM, so every byte counts.MacTCP is wonderful, but it is old, and on a 4 MB Mac Classic with a SCSI Wi-Fi/Ethernet adapter like

A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways.
